title: Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable stock of robotic modules that can rearrange into several useful, load-bearing machines. The same collective would sequentially become a locomotor, a manipulator that moves a useful load, and a freestanding load-supporting structure, then disassemble into stock that can be used again. It would also restore its tested functions after local module failure through reconfiguration or module replacement. These are proposed integrated capabilities, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

The technical idea is to make a collective behave both as a solid that carries loads and as a material whose constituent units can move relative to one another. Devlin and colleagues’ 2025 work provides a demonstrated basis: controlling tangential forces between tightly packed units permits local transitions between rigid and fluid-like behavior. The larger innovation would integrate that behavior with useful actuation, coordinated machine operation, repeatable transformations and recovery after damage.

The scope includes replacing damaged modules from an available supply. It does not require producing replacement modules from raw feedstock, discovering the optimal body for an arbitrary task, or matching every specialized machine’s speed and precision. Those are separate extensions. The defining target is useful functional diversity and repair from a common module stock at explicitly stated human-scale dimensions and loads.

significance.text: If demonstrated, this capability would change the relationship between a robot’s parts and its purpose. Conventional monolithic robots generally retain a designed physical architecture; the proposed collective could use the same parts for substantially different machine functions. Reversible assembly and component reuse already have a technical basis in modular robotics. Combining them with useful loading, active operation and recovery would make morphology itself a reusable resource.

The direct consequence of the proposed demonstration would be that one stock supplies several tested functions and recovers those functions after specified local failures. A possible downstream application is field equipment that changes role instead of requiring a separate vehicle, arm and supporting structure to be transported. Real reductions in equipment shipments would additionally depend on performance, transformation time, power requirements, spare-module needs, reliability and environmental tolerance. A successful laboratory demonstration would not by itself establish those deployment benefits.

The material analogy has useful limits. The 2025 collective demonstrates controllable rigidity and rearrangement, but those behaviors do not alone establish a vehicle, a load-moving arm or a shelter. Likewise, reported healing does not automatically establish recovery of an actively operating machine after a disabled module. The revolutionary step proposed here is integrating these properties into reusable working systems. It belongs broadly to self-reconfiguring and self-repairing hardware, although equivalence to any particular historical benchmark cannot be established from the supplied material.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target integration is a collective that supports stated human-scale loads while rearranging its bulk into several different working machines and restoring function after local damage. Strength and flow are not categorically incompatible: the 2025 collective already combines them through controlled interunit forces. The remaining challenge defined by this proposal is to combine load capacity, controlled rearrangement, actuation and precision across multiple useful configurations. The supplied evidence does not establish whether that complete capability remains undemonstrated across the field as of November 1, 2026.

Connections must provide adequate stiffness and strength while still permitting controlled release, movement and reconnection. During transformation, changing contacts and load paths must remain compatible with the collective’s ability to support itself and move its units. In the specific lattice approach studied by Abdel-Rahman and colleagues in 2022, stronger and stiffer joints and integration at scale remained future work. That supports a concrete engineering barrier in that system, rather than a universal claim that strong modular structures cannot reconfigure.

Engineering synthesis: forming a recognizable shape is insufficient for forming a working machine. A locomotor must generate controlled motion; a manipulator must transmit forces and position a useful load; a freestanding structure must maintain a stable load path. Recovery must restore the relevant function despite the failed unit, rather than merely close a gap or produce another shape. Coordinating those functions, transformations and failure responses using the same module type is the central integration problem.

Practical boundaries also need explicit treatment. Power delivery, control arrangements, external intervention and replacement-module supply affect what autonomy and repair mean. Outdoor durability, high-speed precision and long-duration operation may remain later engineering work, but the proposed demonstration still needs bounded operating conditions and sufficiently reliable performance to make its claimed functions meaningful.

current_state.text: Matthew R. Devlin, Sangwoo Kim, Otger Campàs and Elliot W. Hawkes reported “Material-like robotic collectives with spatiotemporal control of strength and shape” in Science 387, 880–885, on February 21, 2025. The repository abstract retained in the supplied review reports structure formation, healing and a collective supporting 700 newtons, described as 500 times the weight of one robot, before transitioning to flow under its own weight. It attributes rearrangement to modulation of interunit tangential forces. The 500-fold comparison is to an individual robot’s weight, not the collective’s weight, and the described melting is controlled behavior rather than necessarily a load-induced failure.

The evidence available for that result is an identified repository abstract, not retained full article text. It supports the reported load and behaviors but does not supply their experimental conditions or establish the earlier claim of a 20-robot hardware demonstration. No Science article-body artifact was retained to verify the alleged 20-unit sentence or its reported extraction and refetch history. The retained YouTube page identifies a Matt Devlin talk by title but contains no transcript or video evidence supporting the hardware count, account attribution or claimed posting date. The count therefore remains unverified in this record; that limitation is not evidence that it is false.

Abdel-Rahman and colleagues’ 2022 paper, “Self-replicating hierarchical modular robotic swarms,” presents a modular lattice toolkit and a route toward recursive and hierarchical assembly. Its physical components must be distinguished from hierarchy evaluated through simulation and larger assembler robots presented as conceptual designs. The authors leave integration at scale and improved joint stiffness and strength for future work. Their accompanying review exchange also clarifies that the presented algorithm addresses construction rather than reconfiguration. The work therefore should not be described as a physical demonstration of the complete hierarchical, reconfigurable system.

The 2022 paper describes the preceding modular systems it discusses as laboratory demonstrations. That observation applies to those examples in their historical context, not to every modular robotic system through 2026. Neither the reviewed 2022 texts nor the retained 2025 abstract demonstrates the proposed sequence of locomotion, useful-load manipulation, freestanding load support and recovery after module failure from one reusable stock. Uninspected videos and figures cannot establish additional achievements here, and the supplied review contains no bounded freshness search establishing field-wide status as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: use one module type and the same stock to sequentially form three machines without external scaffolding—a locomotor, a manipulator that moves a stated useful load, and a freestanding structure that supports a stated load. Declare dimensions for each configuration so that human scale has a measurable meaning. These choices are proposed acceptance criteria for this innovation, not standards established by the cited papers.
completion_criteria.label: Single-type stock sequentially forms three unscaffolded machines with declared dimensions

completion_criteria.text: Before testing, specify each machine’s functional task, operating duration and acceptable performance, including loads where applicable. The locomotor must demonstrate controlled travel; the manipulator must move its stated load through a declared task; the structure must support its stated load for the declared duration. Shape change alone, even involving a few dozen large units, would not satisfy this proposal because it does not establish the required functions.
completion_criteria.label: Locomotor, manipulator and structure meet their pre-specified performance

completion_criteria.text: Disable a module in each configuration and demonstrate restoration of that configuration’s tested function through reconfiguration or module replacement. Report the failure locations and modes, restoration time, any human intervention and any replacement-module supply. Then return the collective to reusable stock and form the machines again. This sequence would distinguish functional recovery and repeatable reuse from a one-time assembly or a visually healed structure.
completion_criteria.label: Functions restored after each module disablement and reformation from stock

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, disclose module design, power and control arrangements, transformation procedures, test conditions, measurement methods and unsuccessful trials. Repeat the sequence and enable independent replication of the declared functions and failure responses. Report practical boundaries, including tethering, external computation, supporting surfaces, environmental conditions and limits on failures the system can tolerate. Finite tests would establish breadth across the demonstrated configurations and conditions, not universal ability to become any machine or recover from any damage.
completion_criteria.label: Disclosed repeated sequence enables replication within reported practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope synthesis: ROB-04, “Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock,” concerns creating robotic material or replacement modules from feedstock. ROB-05 concerns rearranging and reusing an existing stock, with replacement modules permitted from a declared supply. Producing its own replacements would connect the two capabilities, but module replacement alone does not demonstrate closed-loop reproduction. Only ROB-04’s title was supplied, so this boundary remains an interpretation of the roster rather than a verified comparison with its full specification.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ROB-08, “Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material,” overlaps in collective coordination and structural construction. ROB-05 emphasizes the collective’s own modules becoming reusable machines; ROB-08 emphasizes construction from bulk material. ROB-03, “An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot,” could provide an actuation technology, but a successful actuator would not establish multifunctional reconfiguration, and this proposal does not require a particular artificial muscle.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ROB-01, “Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments,” concerns dependable task execution across unfamiliar settings. ROB-02, “Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability,” concerns manipulation skill and reliability. ROB-05 could provide different bodies for those tasks, but its proposed useful-load manipulator does not establish either broader capability. ROB-07, “Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation,” could help reason about changing contacts and forces during operation or transformation; it remains a distinct predictive-planning capability.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ROB-09, “Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills,” could help a collective retain control skills across configurations, but ROB-05’s demonstration could use predesigned bodies and controllers. ROB-06, “Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body,” and ROB-10, “Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients,” address medical operation at different scales and scopes. Human-scale load-bearing reconfiguration would establish neither internal intervention nor surgical competence. These roster entries remain separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: Whether the complete integrated capability has been demonstrated elsewhere by November 1, 2026 remains unassessed.
The 2025 hardware count, detailed load-test conditions and precise scope of healing cannot be established from the retained abstract and talk-page text.
The alleged Science body sentence, failed-refetch history and talk posting date remain unverified.
Numerical dimensions, loads, operating durations, performance tolerances and permitted intervention still need to be chosen for the proposed demonstration.
The full ROB-04 specification was not supplied; its relationship to ROB-05 is provisionally drawn from its title and the candidate’s stated boundary.
No supplied historical benchmark permits verification of the claimed historical equivalence.

brief.title: Reusable robot parts that become different machines
possible: One set of robot parts could become a moving machine, then an arm that moves a useful load, then a freestanding support. The parts could come apart and form those machines again.
If a part failed, the machine could rearrange itself or use a replacement part to recover its function.
why: The same equipment could serve several purposes. Field teams could potentially carry a reusable stock of parts that changes roles, reducing the need to transport separate machines.

sources.who: Amira Abdel-Rahman, Christopher Cameron, Benjamin Jenett and colleagues
sources.showed: They developed modular building blocks and assembly algorithms. Assembly of larger robots was studied through simulations and conceptual designs, with stronger joints and integration at scale left for future work.
sources.quote: The component composition is supported by an algorithm to compile the building blocks into swarms and plan the optimal construction path.
sources.cited_for: The work supports assembling and reusing common building blocks.
sources.not_established: The remaining step is an integrated physical system that changes between working machines and recovers after part failure.

sources.who: Matthew R. Devlin, Sangwoo Kim, Otger Campàs and Elliot W. Hawkes
sources.showed: This research paper reports robotic collectives that form structures, heal and support loads before switching to flow under their own weight.
sources.cited_for: The work supports combining load-bearing strength with controlled rearrangement.
sources.not_established: Useful machine operation, repeated transformations and functional recovery after a disabled part remain to be demonstrated together.

sources.who: Matthew R. Devlin, Sangwoo Kim, Otger Campàs and Elliot W. Hawkes
sources.showed: A later version of the same work.

shown: Devlin and colleagues demonstrated a tightly packed group of robots that forms structures, heals and supports a load before flowing under its own weight. They control forces between neighbouring parts to switch regions between rigid and fluid-like behaviour.
missing: The same stock still needs to become a moving machine, a load-moving arm and a freestanding support at stated human-scale sizes.
Each form needs to perform its task reliably under stated loads and operating conditions.
The machines need to recover their tested functions after part failure, then come apart and repeat the sequence.

milestones.label: One stock forms each required machine without scaffolding
milestones.explanation: The same stock of one part type would have to form a moving machine, a load-moving arm and a freestanding support, with stated dimensions and loads. This would establish useful forms at a measurable human scale.

milestones.label: Each machine meets its declared performance
milestones.explanation: Each machine would have to meet performance and duration targets set before testing, including controlled travel, load movement and load support. This would establish that each form performs its intended job.

milestones.label: Functions recover after failure and machines form again
milestones.explanation: Each form would have to regain its tested function after a part is disabled, with repairs and assistance reported, then return to stock and form again. This would establish recovery and repeatable reuse.

milestones.label: Repeated results can be independently reproduced
milestones.explanation: Repeated tests would have to disclose designs, power, control, procedures, conditions, measurements and failures so others can reproduce the results. This would establish performance within stated practical limits.

uncertain: The required dimensions, loads, operating durations, precision and permitted human assistance still need to be chosen.
Whether the demonstrated healing can restore an operating machine after a part is disabled remains an open question.

page.title: Load-bearing self-reconfigurable modular robots
page.definition: A reusable stock of robotic modules changes its connections to form machines for different tasks, carries loads during their operation, and returns to stock. Reconfiguration or module replacement restores task performance after component failure.

goal.need: A robotic collective supported 700 N, equivalent to 500 times one robot's weight, in work published on 21 February 2025. Making load-bearing modules reusable across machine functions and replaceable after failure connects that demonstrated force capacity to the field's stated goals of sharing one module stock across machines and recovering from damage.

statements.quote: an entire toolbox originating from a single material form
statements.context: Programme manager Mitchell R. Zakin described the intended equipment capability in a government report dated 15 October 2009.

statements.body: Yim and colleagues, synthesising the Robotics: Science and Systems workshop community
statements.quote: a range of complex machines can be made from one set of modules

statements.body: Devlin and colleagues, developers of material-like robotic collectives
statements.quote: The collective must be strong, to support loads, yet flow, to take new forms.

completion.title: One module stock reforms into load-bearing machines and restores their functions after module failure.
completion.criterion: The same stock forms machines for different tasks, supports external loads during their operation, disassembles into reusable modules, and forms the machines again. Following constituent-module failure, autonomous reconfiguration or module replacement restores the affected machine's demonstrated task performance. Physical hardware must complete this combined cycle. Loads, dimensions, task tolerances and permitted intervention must be specified for the demonstration; the sources establish no common numerical minima.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no published acceptance test for the combined capability was located.
completion.basis: Searches of DARPA's Programmable Matter solicitation, the modular-robotics grand challenges, robotics reviews, and standards and benchmark literature found separate assembly, stiffness, application and repair goals, but no test combining them. This criterion combines those published goals without adding an unsupported machine count, dimension, load or duration.

milestones.title: One particle stock forms four solids, each about 100 cm³, under external command.
milestones.criterion: Particles no larger than 1 cm assemble, under external command, into a cube, cylinder, sphere and triangular prism, each approximately 100 cm³, using one stock. Abdel-Rahman et al., published on 22 November 2022, demonstrated assembly and locomotion; hierarchical construction was evaluated in simulation.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, BAA 07-21 Addendum 7, Phase II; specified for mesoscale particles.

milestones.title: Particle bonds provide 0.2–4 GPa bulk elastic modulus and then release the original particles.
milestones.criterion: Particle interlocking produces bulk elastic modulus of 0.2–4 GPa, followed by release of the original particles. Smith et al.'s 2024 ICRA paper reports one 27-voxel aluminium lattice specimen with compressive modulus 5.1 MPa and maximum compressive load 4576.68 N. This different architecture does not establish the DARPA particle test.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, BAA 07-21 Addendum 7, Phase II; specified for mesoscale particles.
milestones.threshold_quote: (0.2 to 4 GPa), followed by unlocking to recover the original particles.

milestones.title: A modular robot autonomously recovers after internal failure or separation into pieces.
milestones.criterion: A physical modular system autonomously reassembles after random separation into pieces, or recovers from internal module failures. The published challenge fixes no faulty-module percentage. Devlin et al.'s abstract reports healing without a module-disablement protocol. Cordie et al., published on 13 March 2024, demonstrated continued locomotion after removal of a failed drive module; decoupling was manual. Their physical current measurements report n = 12.
milestones.set_by: Yim and colleagues' community grand challenge, published in IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine; not an IEEE standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: recover from failure of a certain percentage of faulty units.

milestones.title: One module stock forms machines for different tasks and disassembles into reusable modules.
milestones.criterion: One module stock forms machines that execute different tasks, then disassembles into modules that can form those machines again. DARPA stated an application goal but deferred application-specific Phase III criteria. Cai et al., published on 19 August 2026, demonstrated a three-module crawler changing into a snake and retrieving an object, using an offline reconfiguration plan; their reported demonstration does not establish this complete reuse cycle.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of DARPA Phase III criteria, modular-robotics benchmarks and standards found no common functional-reuse test.

not_found: No publication was located demonstrating the complete combined cycle of loaded machine operation, stock reuse and restoration of task performance after module failure.
DARPA explicitly deferred application-specific Phase III acceptance criteria.
The 2025 Science article and supplements could not be opened, leaving load-test specimen count, geometry and duration unverified.
DARPA's original solicitation URL was unavailable; its notice text was opened in GovTribe's reproduction.

results.finding: Two four-cube assemblies formed a 3D stack in all 5 trials using 2 mm modules.
results.detail: The assemblies were controlled by a global magnetic field. The source does not demonstrate all four required solids at approximately 100 cm³ from one stock.
results.quote:
Under the actuation conditions used in Fig.
5
\(\left(\alpha ={60}^{\circ },\,\Delta \theta =\pm {30}^{\circ }\right)\)
, successful vertical stacking was observed in all 5 trials.

results.finding: One 15-module CKbot robot reassembled from 3 randomly scattered clusters and resumed walking; number of trials not stated.
results.detail: A kick separated the robot at magnetic connections. The clusters self-righted, searched for one another and docked before the robot stood and resumed walking.
results.quote:
Fig. 1: Three piece self-reassembly after explosion. a) kick to midsection, b) resulting in three clusters of modules strewn randomly, c) clusters 
self-right and dock, d) system stands up, 3) system resumes walking.

results.finding: An MNS robot recovered from an injected body-unit fault by recruiting 2 replacement units; trial count not reported.
results.detail: Eight robotic units were used in the self-healing demonstration. The failed body part detached, and the replacement units recreated the original robot under predefined behavioral rules.
results.quote: In this case, the body part containing the failed unit is detached from the MNS robot and two new robotic units are recruited to recreate the original robot (Supplementary Fig.

results.finding: Four s-bots encountered a bridge and then a gap in one proof-of-concept experiment.
results.detail: The source describes obstacle-specific formations and disassembly, but does not report the outcome of the combined experiment or establish that both machines were formed again after disassembly.
results.quote:
We conducted 5 experiments in which two robots encoun-
tered the bridge, 5 experiments in which four robots en-
countered the gap, and a proof of concept experiment in
which four robots encountered ﬁrst the bridge and then the
gap.

results.finding: SMORES-EP modules formed task-specific configurations in 3 hardware demonstrations.
results.detail: The same modules were used across demonstrations, and configurations were changed and changed back. The text does not establish disassembly into a reusable stock and subsequent reassembly of the machines.
results.quote: It should be noted that all experiments were run using the same software architecture, same SMORES-EP modules, and system described in this paper.

results.finding: Modular material-robot hardware used 101.6 mm voxels; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The paper reports robotic assembly and locomotion, but the voxels exceed the 1 cm limit. It does not demonstrate assembly of all four specified solids from one stock.
results.quote:
The fully assembled voxel forms a 101.6 mm (4 in.) cube and weighs 65 grams, resulting in a lattice with an effective density of 0.062 g/cm
3
.

results.finding: A robotic collective supported 700 N before melting; sample size was not reported.
results.detail: The source reports load support and a transition to a fluid-like state, but gives no bulk elastic modulus or demonstration that the original particles were released.
results.quote: We demonstrate structure-forming and healing and show the collective supporting 700 newtons (500 times the weight of a robot) before “melting” under its own weight.

results.finding: A robotic collective demonstrated healing; sample size and the number of failures were not reported.
results.detail: The abstract does not describe a module failure or random separation, or establish that recovery was autonomous.
results.quote: We demonstrate structure-forming and healing and show the collective supporting 700 newtons (500 times the weight of a robot) before “melting” under its own weight.

results.finding: Two L-shaped assemblies separated and reconfigured into a W-shaped structure at 72 s; trial count not stated.
results.detail: The assemblies remained intact during separation. The demonstration does not establish different task execution or disassembly into individual reusable modules followed by rebuilding the machines.
results.quote: The two structures are then reoriented within the planar workspace between 70 s and 72 s and guided into a new configuration, resulting in the formation of a planar W-shaped structure at 72 s.

results.finding: One 15-module robot separated into three clusters, reassembled and resumed walking.
results.detail: The demonstration restored one walking machine after disassembly. It did not show the same stock forming machines for different tasks and reforming them after disassembly.
results.quote:
Fig. 1: Three piece self-reassembly after explosion. a) kick to midsection, b) resulting in three clusters of modules strewn randomly, c) clusters 
self-right and dock, d) system stands up, 3) system resumes walking.

results.finding: In one experiment, 10 robotic units formed composite robots that reacted to a stimulus.
results.detail: The robots merged into different configurations and coordinated pointing and retreating. The source does not demonstrate the complete cycle of forming machines for different tasks, disassembling them, and forming those machines again.
results.quote: The different MNS robots all display the same coordinated sensorimotor reaction to a provided stimulus.

results.finding: Reversibly assembled composite lattice, sample size not stated: measured bulk modulus 12.3 MPa.
results.detail: The modulus is below the 0.2–4 GPa target. The paper describes reversible links, but the supplied text does not report releasing the original parts after the modulus test.
results.quote:
The resulting cellular composite materials can respond as an elastic solid
with an extremely large measured modulus for an ultralight material (12.3 megapascals at a
density of 7.2 milligrams per cubic centimeter).

results.finding: Two 8-module robot configurations were repeatedly assembled and disassembled 10 times.
results.detail: An external manipulator performed the reconfiguration, and disassembly required manual position corrections. The experiments did not report the configurations executing different tasks or a complete task-and-reuse cycle.
